articleBlocks: At first, the puzzle felt scattered. Some names seemed mythic, others vaguely scientific.
Titan, Triton, and even Phobos have strong mythological associations.
I was initially drawn to a 'Mythological Figures' theme, but Io and Ganymede felt out of place.
The clue about Galileo observing Ganymede was the turning point.
It shifted the focus to astronomy and early observations.
Suddenly, the answer snapped into focus: Moons in our solar system.
Each name represents a moon orbiting a planet in our solar system.
Titan orbits Saturn. Triton orbits Neptune.
Phobos orbits Mars. Io and Ganymede orbit Jupiter.
The Galileo clue was essential, providing the context to connect the mythological names to specific moons.
Looking back, the Galileo clue was the key to pinpointing the exact category.
Now the puzzle feels obvious in hindsight.
solutionNarrative: Titan and Triton first pulled me toward Greek Gods, so that was the first path I tested. It held together for a moment, but phobos never really fit it. The more I pushed that first read, the more the board sounded stitched together instead of naturally solved.

The solve turned when I stopped treating phobos as just another clue and asked what kind of thing each clue could really be describing. Once I made that shift, I was no longer thinking about Greek Gods; I was checking whether the earlier clues all behaved like parts of the same real set. That was when the answer became clear, because the remaining clues stopped feeling like separate trivia and started reinforcing the real category.
